title: Gene Expression and Biotechnology
seo_title: Year 13 A Level Biology: Gene Expression and Biotechnology Worksheets
standard_code: A level Biology: The control of gene expression
standard_text: Gene mutations, stem cells, regulation of transcription and translation, epigenetics, gene expression and cancer, genome projects, recombinant DNA technology, PCR, DNA probes, genetic screening, gene therapy and genetic fingerprinting.
meta_desc: Free Year 13 A level biology worksheets on gene expression: stem cells, transcription factors, epigenetics, cancer, PCR, restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis and genetic fingerprinting. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: PCR doubles the DNA every cycle: copies = start × 2ⁿ.
key_sub: Small DNA fragments travel furthest in a gel.
body_html:
How to think about it

Genes are switched on and off by transcription factors, RNA interference and epigenetic changes (DNA methylation, histone acetylation). Mutations in tumour suppressor genes and proto-oncogenes can cause uncontrolled cell division.

Recombinant DNA: cut with restriction enzymes to leave sticky ends, join into a vector with DNA ligase, and use marker genes to find transformed cells. PCR copies DNA: start × 2ⁿ after n cycles. Gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size.

Example

10 molecules, 5 PCR cycles. Molecules?

10 × 2⁵

Answer: 320

Example

1,000 bp cut at 300 and 700. Fragments?

300, 400, 300

Answer: 400 and 300 bp

Common mistakes

  • Multiplying by 2 × n instead of 2ⁿ.
  • Thinking large fragments move furthest.
  • Thinking epigenetic changes alter the base sequence.

faq.a: A protein that binds to DNA near a gene and switches its transcription on or off.

faq.q: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
faq.a: It comes from bacteria in hot springs and is not denatured at the 95 °C used to separate DNA strands.

items.q: Why can different cells in one body make different proteins?
c: different genes are switched on (expressed) in each cell type
items.e: All body cells have the same genome.

items.q: What is the difference between benign and malignant tumours?
c: malignant tumours invade tissues and spread (metastasis)
benign tumours spread around the body
items.e: Benign tumours are usually enclosed.

items.q: What is a unipotent stem cell?
c: one that can become any cell
one that can only become one type of cell
items.e: For example cardiomyocytes from heart stem cells.

items.q: mRNA: GAAACUGUU. Codons: ACU = Thr, GAA = Glu, GUU = Val, UUU = Phe. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: GAA ACU GUU.

items.q: What is a gene mutation called that adds an extra base?
items.e: It causes a frameshift.

items.q: What is a stem cell?
c: an undifferentiated cell that can divide and become specialised
items.e: Totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent cells.

items.q: mRNA: GAUGGUUGG. Codons: GAU = Asp, GGU = Gly, UGG = Trp, ACU = Thr, UCU = Ser. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: GAU GGU UGG.

items.q: mRNA: UUCGAAUAU. Codons: GAA = Glu, UAU = Tyr, UUC = Phe, UGU = Cys, GCU = Ala. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: UUC GAA UAU.

items.q: What does an inversion mutation do?
items.e: The bases are the same but in reverse order.

items.q: mRNA: CAUGGCGAA. Codons: CAU = His, GAA = Glu, GGC = Gly, UCU = Ser, AGC = Ser. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: CAU GGC GAA.

items.q: What is a transcription factor?
c: an enzyme that joins amino acids
a protein that binds to DNA and switches transcription of a gene on or off
items.e: It binds near the gene's promoter.

items.q: mRNA: AUUGGUAAA. Codons: AAA = Lys, AUU = Ile, GGU = Gly, UUU = Phe, UGU = Cys. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AUU GGU AAA.

items.q: mRNA: UUCUUCACU. Codons: ACU = Thr, UUC = Phe, GCA = Ala, CGU = Arg. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: UUC UUC ACU.

items.q: How does oestrogen switch on a gene?
c: it diffuses into the cell and binds to a receptor, releasing a transcription factor
items.e: The factor can then bind to DNA.

items.q: mRNA: AGCAGCUGU. Codons: AGC = Ser, UGU = Cys, AUG = Met. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AGC AGC UGU.

items.q: What is the genome of an organism?
items.e: The proteome is the set of proteins it can make.

items.q: mRNA: CGUAAAUUC. Codons: AAA = Lys, CGU = Arg, UUC = Phe, GCU = Ala, GUU = Val. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: CGU AAA UUC.

items.q: What is an ethical issue with embryonic stem cells?
c: embryos are destroyed to obtain them
items.e: iPS cells avoid this.

items.q: What does siRNA do?
c: guides an enzyme to cut a complementary mRNA
items.e: The mRNA cannot then be translated.

items.q: mRNA: CUUGAUUGG. Codons: CUU = Leu, GAU = Asp, UGG = Trp, CAU = His, ACU = Thr. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: CUU GAU UGG.

items.q: What is a tumour suppressor gene?
c: a gene that makes cells divide faster
a gene that slows cell division; if mutated, cells can divide uncontrollably
a gene that only works in plants
items.e: For example the gene for p53.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence GCCCAGAGGC. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence TCGATTATCAAC. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence TCAGCTATTT. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: What is epigenetics?
c: heritable changes in gene function without changes to the base sequence
items.e: For example DNA methylation.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence AGTTGAGGTAAC. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: How does increased methylation of DNA affect a gene?
c: it stops transcription factors binding, so the gene is switched off
items.e: Methyl groups are added to cytosine.

items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence CGGTTGGCAA. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: Why is it harder to find the proteome from the genome in complex organisms?
c: non-coding DNA and regulatory genes make it hard to predict the proteins
items.e: Alternative splicing also adds proteins.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence GTTACGTGGCGG. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence TCGGCAGAAACG. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: How does decreased acetylation of histones affect a gene?
c: the chromatin becomes more condensed, so transcription is inhibited
items.e: Acetylation loosens chromatin.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence AAGTCGCCCGTG. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: How can a substitution mutation stop a protein working?
c: it may change an amino acid in the active site so the shape changes
it always makes the protein longer
items.e: Or it may create a stop codon.

items.q: Which stem cells can become any type of cell, including placenta?
items.e: Found in the early embryo.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence TTCAGCACCTAC. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence GCTGTGATGG. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: A DNA probe is needed to bind to the base sequence GTGAATTG. What is the probe's sequence?
items.e: A probe is a short single strand complementary to the target: A–T, G–C.

items.q: What is genetic screening used for?
c: finding people who carry particular alleles
items.e: Genetic counselling then explains the risks.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 3,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 200. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 3,000): 2,800, 200. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 3,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1,300, 2,050. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 3,000): 1,300, 950, 750. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: Why are bacteria treated with calcium ions and heat shock in genetic engineering?
c: to make the cell wall and membrane more permeable to plasmids
items.e: This is transformation.

items.q: What are primers in PCR?
c: RNA molecules that carry amino acids
short single strands of DNA that bind to the start of the target sequence
items.e: DNA polymerase starts from them.

items.q: Why are marker genes used in genetic engineering?
c: to identify cells that have taken up the recombinant DNA
to make the gene work faster
items.e: For example antibiotic resistance or fluorescence.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 250, 550. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1,000): 450, 300, 250. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1,200. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2,000): 1,200, 800. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1,200 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 150, 750. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1,200): 600, 450, 150. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What is a sticky end?
c: a short single-stranded overhang left by some restriction enzymes
items.e: Complementary sticky ends can join.

items.q: What is needed for PCR?
c: DNA, primers, free nucleotides and Taq DNA polymerase
items.e: A thermal cycler changes the temperature.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 3,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 300, 450. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 3,000): 2,550, 300, 150. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What is a DNA probe used for?
c: finding a specific allele by binding to a complementary sequence
items.e: Probes are labelled with fluorescent or radioactive markers.

items.q: What does in vivo gene cloning use?
c: vectors such as plasmids to put genes into host cells
items.e: In vitro cloning uses PCR.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1,300, 1,500. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2,000): 1,300, 500, 200. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: Why is PCR heated to about 95 °C?
c: to separate the DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
items.e: Primers anneal at about 55 °C; extension at 72 °C.

items.q: How does gel electrophoresis separate DNA fragments?
c: by size: smaller fragments move further towards the positive electrode
items.e: DNA is negatively charged.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2,400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 2,150. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2,400): 2,150, 250. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 3,000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 700. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 3,000): 2,300, 700. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: How can genetically modified bacteria make human insulin?
c: bacteria are fused with human cells
the human insulin gene is put into a plasmid and inserted into the bacteria
items.e: The bacteria are grown in fermenters.

items.q: What do restriction endonucleases do?
c: cut DNA at specific recognition sequences
items.e: Many leave sticky ends.

items.q: What does DNA ligase do?
c: joins sugar–phosphate backbones of DNA fragments
items.e: It seals sticky ends together.

items.q: PCR starts with 50 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 12 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 50 × 212 = 204,800.

items.q: PCR starts with 5 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 8 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 5 × 28 = 1,280.

items.q: What is gene therapy?
c: inserting a working allele into cells to treat a genetic disorder
items.e: Somatic therapy is not passed to children.

items.q: PCR starts with 50 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 3 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 50 × 23 = 400.

items.q: PCR starts with 5 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 5 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 5 × 25 = 160.

items.q: What does reverse transcriptase do?
c: makes cDNA from an mRNA template
items.e: Used to make genes without introns.

items.q: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
c: it is not denatured at high temperatures
items.e: It comes from a bacterium in hot springs.

items.q: PCR starts with 100 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 3 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 100 × 23 = 800.

items.q: PCR starts with 10 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 15 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 10 × 215 = 327,680.

items.q: Why is a promoter added with a gene in genetic engineering?
c: so RNA polymerase can bind and the gene is transcribed
items.e: A terminator is added to stop it.

items.q: What is genetic fingerprinting based on?
c: variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs), which differ between people
genes that are the same in everyone
items.e: The pattern of bands is compared.

items.q: PCR starts with 20 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 8 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 20 × 28 = 5,120.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 4 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 80 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 20 cycles; amount × 220 = 1,048,576.

items.e: 25 cycles; amount × 225 = 33,554,432.

items.q: PCR starts with 3 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 20 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 3 × 220 = 3,145,728.

items.q: What is an ethical concern about genetically modified crops?
c: genes could spread to wild plants, and there may be less biodiversity
items.e: Benefits include higher yields and pest resistance.

items.q: Why are the same restriction enzymes used to cut the gene and the plasmid?

so they have complementary sticky ends
items.e: The ends can then base pair.
